query: For multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, what single testable methodological intervention could overcome the inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid? Explain why it should improve reference–target phase-space overlap, predict the reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, define the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations, and specify a decisive free-energy benchmark that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing traditional EAM references with an actively‐learned machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) (e.g., a moment tensor or deep neural network potential) will better capture the multiplicity of atomic configurations in the ab initio liquid state of multicomponent high‐entropy alloys. This improved reference will yield enhanced phase‐space overlap and a reduced thermodynamic‐integration path mismatch compared to TOR-TILD’s EAM references.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high‐entropy alloys (e.g., refractory, equimolar alloys with ≥5 principal elements) in both their solid and liquid states near the high melting temperature (typically at temperatures close to the melting point, e.g. T ≳0.8Tm).
generation.intervention: Develop and use an MLIP—trained on a diverse set of ab initio configurations representing both the disordered liquid and solid phases—as the reference potential in thermodynamic integration calculations.
generation.conditions: Applicable for high-entropy alloys with complex, chemically disordered mixtures (such as refractory alloys) where the liquid state has a vast configuration space; temperature conditions should be near the melting temperature where entropy plays a dominant role.
generation.structural_mediator: The MLIP, by accurately learning many-body interactions and configurational variability from ab initio data, mediates between the target ab initio phase space and the integration reference, ensuring a closer overlap of explored configurations.
generation.mechanism: Unlike EAM potentials, which are unable to represent the broad configurational diversity of the ab initio liquid, the MLIP explicitly learns from representative atomic configurations. This ensures that when used as a reference in thermodynamic integration, the MLIP follows a smoother path with reduced energetic discontinuities (mismatch) between reference and target states.
generation.predicted_outcome: The MLIP-based reference is expected to reduce the integration path mismatch by a significant amount (on the order of 30-50% or more, though the exact figure is uncertain) relative to the TOR-TILD’s EAM references, yielding free-energy estimates that deviate by only a few meV per atom from direct ab initio AIMD benchmarks.
generation.baseline: Existing TOR-TILD calculations using EAM references that show marked phase-space gaps due to their limited ability to represent the many atomic configurations of the liquid state.
generation.boundary: This approach is most applicable to multicomponent HEAs at high temperatures near their melting points. Its performance may be less certain in systems with strong local chemical ordering or where high-quality training data for the MLIP is sparse.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative reduction in the mismatch of the thermodynamic integration path remains uncertain and will depend on the alloy chemistry, the range of configurations sampled, and the quality of the ML training dataset.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative refractory high-entropy alloy and perform parallel thermodynamic integration to determine the free energy difference between its solid and liquid phases using (i) the conventional TOR-TILD approach with an EAM reference and (ii) the new MLIP-based reference. Independently, perform ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) free-energy calculations to establish a benchmark.
measurements: Free energy differences between solid and liquid states
Metrics quantifying the integration path mismatch (e.g., energy fluctuations along the path)
Convergence properties and computational efficiency of the integration path
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the MLIP-based reference does not yield free energy differences that are closer to the AIMD benchmark (e.g., within ±5 meV/atom) and does not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction (at least ≈30% improvement) in the integration path mismatch compared to the EAM-based method, then the hypothesis will be falsified.
